sections.heading: Structure of the heart
sections.specBullet: Structure and function of the heart

paragraphs: The heart is a muscular double pump divided down the middle by the septum. Each side has an upper atrium and a lower ventricle. The atria only push blood a short distance into the ventricles below, so their walls are thin; the ventricles push blood out of the heart entirely, so theirs are thick.
The left ventricle has the thickest wall of all four chambers. It has to generate enough pressure to supply the whole body, while the right ventricle only pushes blood as far as the lungs.

items.meaning: The muscular wall dividing the heart into a left and a right side.

A lower chamber of the heart, contracting to force blood out of the heart.

Out of the left ventricle to the body

paragraphs: Four valves keep blood moving one way only. Each opens to let blood through, then closes to stop it running back.

items.right: It is the exception. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood back.

sections.heading: Control of heart rate
sections.specBullet: Neural and hormonal regulation of heart rate

paragraphs: The heart sets its own beat, but the speed of that beat is adjusted moment to moment by the cardiac control centre in the medulla oblongata, through both nervous and hormonal pathways.

items.meaning: The area of the medulla oblongata that adjusts heart rate using information from receptors.
Sends impulses to the SAN to speed the heart up.
Sends impulses that slow the heart back down towards its resting rate.
A stress hormone acting directly on the SAN to increase both the speed and the force of each contraction.

paragraphs: Three types of receptor feed information to the cardiac control centre. Each has its own location and its own trigger.

items.meaning: In the carotid arteries and aortic arch, they detect rising carbon dioxide in the blood, triggering greater sympathetic stimulation and a faster heart rate.
In the walls of major arteries, they detect stretch caused by changes in blood pressure - a rise in pressure lowers heart rate, a fall raises it.
In the muscles, tendons and joints, they detect increased movement as exercise begins and pass this to the medulla, raising heart rate.

paragraphs: The baroreceptors have a wrinkle worth knowing. Their normal job is to bring heart rate down when blood pressure rises, which would be unhelpful at the start of exercise. Their set point is temporarily raised instead, so heart rate is not pulled back down exactly when it is needed.

items: Cardiac control centre in the medulla oblongata

Parasympathetic nervous system decreases heart rate

sections.heading: Stroke volume, heart rate and cardiac output
sections.specBullet: Cardiac dynamics and the effect of training

items.meaning: The volume of blood ejected by a ventricle in a single beat, averaging around 70 ml at rest.
The number of times the heart beats each minute, averaging around 72 bpm at rest.
The total volume of blood pumped by the heart in one minute.
The percentage of the blood in the ventricle at the end of filling that is pumped out on the next beat - about 60% at rest, rising to as much as 85% with training.

blocks.equation: Cardiac output = Stroke volume × Heart rate
blocks.meaning: At rest this gives a typical value of around 5 litres per minute.

paragraphs: Stroke volume is set by three things: venous return, the natural elasticity of the cardiac muscle fibres, and the contractility of the heart muscle itself. Venous return is the one that changes most during exercise, and it works through Starling's law.

items.meaning: The natural stretch and recoil of the cardiac muscle fibres.
The force the heart muscle itself can generate when it contracts.
The ceiling heart rate rises to as intensity increases, estimated as 220 minus age.
The point during longer sub-maximal exercise where oxygen supply matches oxygen demand and heart rate levels off.
The enlargement and strengthening of the heart muscle caused by regular aerobic training.
A resting heart rate below 60 bpm, produced by a larger, stronger heart needing fewer beats.

blocks.meaning: An estimate of the ceiling heart rate can reach - so about 203 bpm for a 17-year-old.

paragraphs: Stroke volume only keeps rising to around 40 to 60 percent of maximum effort, then plateaus. As heart rate climbs towards its maximum, the ventricles have less time to fill during diastole, which caps how much can be ejected per beat. Beyond that point, extra cardiac output comes from heart rate alone.

Trained performers have a lower resting heart rate and a higher maximum heart rate, giving a much wider heart rate range. Elite endurance athletes have been recorded resting in the low thirties, against about 72 bpm untrained.

rows: Anticipatory rise before the start, sharp increase once anaerobic work begins, quick fall in recovery

items.right: Resting cardiac output is similar in both. A trained heart delivers it with fewer, bigger beats. It is maximum cardiac output that is substantially higher.

items.wrong: Stroke volume keeps rising all the way to maximal exercise.
items.right: It plateaus at around 40 to 60 percent of maximum, because filling time shortens as heart rate climbs.

paragraphs: Blood pressure falls the further a vessel is from the heart: highest in the aorta, lowest in the veins. sections.heading: Venous return
sections.specBullet: Venous return mechanisms

items.meaning: The flow of blood back into the right side of the heart through the vena cava.
An increase in venous return leads to greater filling and stretching of the heart during diastole, producing a stronger contraction and a greater proportion of blood ejected.

paragraphs: At rest as much as 70 percent of the body's total blood volume is held in the veins, which is a large reserve to call on. But pressure there is very low and the wide lumen offers little resistance, so the body needs active mechanisms to keep blood moving back.

items: Skeletal muscle pump: contracting and relaxing muscles press against nearby veins, squeezing blood towards the heart
Respiratory pump: breathing changes pressure in the chest and abdomen, compressing veins and pushing blood onward
Pocket (one-way) valves: prevent blood flowing backwards once it has passed through
Additional support: smooth muscle in the vein walls, gravity assisting return from the upper body, and a suction effect from the heart itself

paragraphs: At rest the valves and smooth muscle are generally enough on their own. During exercise the skeletal muscle pump and respiratory pump become essential, and both are naturally active anyway, since muscles are contracting and breathing rate is rising. This is why an active cool-down matters: keeping moving keeps those pumps working and prevents blood pooling in the veins.

Blood pressure acts on venous return directly, rising systolic pressure increasing it and falling pressure reducing it. Stated precisely, the driver is a pressure gradient: venous pressure less right atrial pressure, divided by venous vascular resistance.

Because both venous pressure and right atrial pressure are normally very low, even a small change, such as the pressure change in the chest during inspiration, produces a comparatively large change in venous return.

items.wrong: The heart sucks blood back through the veins.
items.right: Suction from the heart plays only a small part. Most of the work is done by the muscle pump, the respiratory pump and the valves.

items: 70 percent of blood volume sits in the veins at rest
Muscle pump, respiratory pump, pocket valves, smooth muscle
More venous return feeds straight into Starling's law

sections.heading: Redistribution of blood: the vascular shunt mechanism
sections.specBullet: Redistribution of blood flow during exercise

items.meaning: The redistribution of blood flow towards the working muscles and away from less essential organs, also called shunting.
The area of the medulla oblongata that coordinates redistribution by adjusting vessel diameter.
The widening of blood vessels to increase flow, in the arterioles supplying the working muscles.
The narrowing of blood vessels to reduce flow, in the arterioles supplying less essential organs such as the intestines and liver.
Small rings of muscle at the entrance to capillaries, relaxing to allow more blood into active tissue and contracting to restrict flow elsewhere.

items: Chemoreceptors detect rising carbon dioxide and lactic acid in the blood

paragraphs: Redistribution serves four purposes at once: more oxygen to the working muscles, removal of waste such as carbon dioxide and lactic acid, extra blood to the skin for temperature regulation, and extra oxygen to the heart muscle itself.
It also has a practical consequence. Eating shortly before competing is best avoided, since a full stomach draws blood towards digestion rather than towards the working muscles.

items.right: Brain flow stays broadly constant and is protected. It is the intestines and kidneys that lose out.

items.wrong: Shunting means the body makes more blood.
items.right: The same blood is redirected. Cardiac output rises separately.

sections.heading: Transport of oxygen
sections.specBullet: Transport of oxygen and the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve

paragraphs: Oxygen is carried in two ways. About 3 percent dissolves directly into the blood plasma; the remaining 97 percent binds to haemoglobin in the red blood cells to form oxyhaemoglobin. When fully saturated, each haemoglobin molecule carries four molecules of oxygen.

items.meaning: The protein in red blood cells that oxygen binds to for transport around the body.
Haemoglobin with oxygen bound to it.
The release of oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin at the tissues, where the partial pressure of oxygen is lower.
Stores oxygen within the muscle, with an even higher affinity for oxygen than haemoglobin, holding it ready for the mitochondria.
The rightward shift of the dissociation curve during exercise, meaning haemoglobin gives up its oxygen more readily at any given partial pressure.

paragraphs: The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve plots percentage saturation of haemoglobin against the partial pressure of oxygen, and its S-shape matters. In the lungs, where partial pressure is high, haemoglobin becomes almost fully saturated. At the tissues, where it is lower, haemoglobin releases part of its load.

sections.heading: Cardiovascular disease and the benefits of exercise
sections.specBullet: Impact of physical activity on cardiovascular health

paragraphs: Coronary heart disease is the leading cause of death in the UK and worldwide. It develops through atherosclerosis, where the coronary arteries supplying the heart muscle gradually narrow and become blocked by fatty deposits. High blood pressure, high cholesterol, physical inactivity and smoking are all risk factors.

items.meaning: Narrowing and blocking of the coronary arteries that supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood.
The process by which the coronary arteries gradually narrow and become blocked by fatty deposits.
The fatty deposit that builds up inside the artery wall.
The chest pain and discomfort caused when narrowed arteries leave the heart muscle short of oxygen.
What happens when a piece of atheroma breaks away and forms a clot blocking a coronary artery entirely, cutting oxygen to part of the heart muscle.

paragraphs: Because the heart is itself a muscle, regular exercise keeps it healthy: bigger, stronger and more efficient, with a greater stroke volume, more flexible blood vessels, normal blood pressure and healthier cholesterol.

items.meaning: Extra strain on the heart and arteries which, untreated, raises the risk of heart attack, heart failure, kidney disease, stroke and dementia.
A fatty substance carried around the body in two main forms, LDL and HDL.

Carries excess cholesterol back to the liver to be broken down. Considered 'good' cholesterol, as it lowers heart disease risk.

paragraphs: Regular aerobic exercise lowers both systolic and diastolic blood pressure, which reduces the risk of a heart attack. It also lowers LDL while raising HDL.

sections.heading: Joint actions in the sagittal plane
sections.specBullet: Joint actions in the sagittal plane

items.meaning: A decrease in the angle around a joint.
An increase in the angle around a joint.
Where the angle increases beyond 180 degrees.
At the ankle: pointing the toes, or pushing up onto the toes.
At the ankle: pulling the toes up towards the shin.

paragraphs: All five syllabus joints - ankle, knee, hip, elbow and shoulder - flex and extend.

The shoulder is an exception to the angle rule. With the arm by the side, raising the arm forward is flexion and lowering it back down is extension. Moving the arm further back, past the side of the body, is hyper-extension.

sections.heading: Joint actions in the frontal and transverse planes
sections.specBullet: Joint actions in the frontal and transverse planes

items.meaning: Movement of a limb away from the midline of the body, such as raising the arms or legs out to the side.
Movement of a limb back towards the midline of the body, such as lowering the arms or legs back to the sides.
Movement of the arm forwards across the body, starting from shoulder abduction with the arm held out to the side, parallel to the floor.
Movement of the arm backwards away from the body, starting from shoulder flexion with the arm held at 90 degrees in front of the body.

items: Abduction takes the limb away from the midline
Adduction adds it back towards the midline
The horizontal versions both start from a different position - note which

sections.heading: Agonist and antagonist muscles
sections.specBullet: Agonist and antagonist muscle pairs

paragraphs: A joint cannot move on its own. When a muscle contracts, one end stays anchored while the other pulls the bone it is attached to, creating movement.

items.meaning: The muscle responsible for causing a movement.
The muscle working in opposition, lengthening as the agonist shortens.
The two working together to produce smooth, controlled movement - as when the biceps contracts as agonist to flex the elbow while the triceps acts as antagonist and lengthens.

items: Reverse the action and the pair swaps roles
The agonist shortens, the antagonist lengthens
Learn them as pairs, not as eighteen separate facts

sections.heading: Types of muscular contraction
sections.specBullet: Types of muscular contraction

items.meaning: A contraction where the muscle produces movement. It comes in two types, concentric and eccentric.
The muscle shortens under tension - the biceps during the upward phase of an arm curl, producing flexion of the elbow.
The muscle lengthens under tension rather than relaxing, acting like a brake to control movement (negative work) - the quadriceps controlling the body on landing from a jump.
The muscle is under tension but does not change length, so no visible movement takes place - holding the crucifix position in gymnastics, or holding a weight still mid-curl.

items.wrong: An eccentric contraction means the muscle is relaxing.
items.right: It is still under tension - it is lengthening against a load, working as a brake.

items.wrong: No movement means no contraction.
items.right: A joint or limb described as still, stationary or held is an isometric contraction: tension without a change in length.

items: Isotonic produces movement; isometric does not
Concentric shortens, eccentric lengthens, both under tension
Still, stationary or held means isometric

sections.heading: ATP and energy transfer
sections.specBullet: ATP as the energy currency of the body

paragraphs: The body needs a constant supply of energy to fuel muscle contraction, whatever the activity. The intensity and duration of that activity decide which energy system supplies it.

items.meaning: The only usable form of chemical energy in the body - one molecule of adenosine bonded to three phosphate groups.
What ATP becomes once the outer phosphate bond is broken and energy released, alongside an inorganic phosphate (Pi).
A reaction where the energy released by one process is immediately used to drive another.

blocks.equation: ATP + energy in ⇌ ADP + Pi + energy out
blocks.meaning: Energy is released when the outer phosphate bond breaks, and resynthesis runs the same reaction in reverse.

paragraphs: Only small amounts of ATP can be stored in the muscle at any time, so it must be continually resynthesised from ADP and Pi during exercise. That resynthesis is fuelled by food - carbohydrate and fat - or by phosphocreatine stored in the muscle.
Three energy systems can resynthesise ATP: the aerobic system, the ATP-PC (phosphocreatine) system, and the anaerobic glycolytic system. Which one predominates depends on intensity and duration.

sections.heading: The aerobic energy system
sections.specBullet: The aerobic energy system

paragraphs: Low intensity, with enough oxygen arriving to meet it, is where this system operates, which makes it the body's default at rest and through long, steady work. Glucose is broken down with oxygen present, leaving carbon dioxide and water behind. Fats serve as fuel too, and protein if it comes to that.

items: Glycolysis: in the sarcoplasm of the muscle cell, glucose is broken down anaerobically into pyruvic acid for a net gain of 2 ATP. With enough oxygen, pyruvic acid becomes acetyl coenzyme A and passes into the mitochondria

The Krebs cycle: in the matrix of the mitochondria, acetyl coenzyme A combines with oxaloacetic acid to form citric acid, producing carbon dioxide as waste, 2 ATP, and hydrogen carried onward by coenzymes

The electron transport chain: in the cristae of the mitochondria, hydrogen is split into electrons and hydrogen ions, releasing energy to resynthesise around 34 ATP, with hydrogen and electrons eventually recombining with oxygen to form water

items.meaning: The anaerobic breakdown of glucose into pyruvic acid in the sarcoplasm, yielding a net 2 ATP.
The stage in the mitochondrial matrix where acetyl coenzyme A combines with oxaloacetic acid, producing carbon dioxide, 2 ATP and hydrogen.
The stage in the cristae where hydrogen is split, releasing energy to resynthesise around 34 ATP and forming water.
Stored fat (triglyceride) is broken into glycerol and free fatty acids, transported in the blood and converted to acetyl coenzyme A so it can enter the Krebs cycle.

paragraphs: Fat metabolism yields more ATP per molecule than glucose, but the process is more complex, needs more oxygen, and cannot run without also breaking down some carbohydrate. It only becomes the predominant fuel in longer, lower-intensity exercise, where a fitter individual has more time to take up and use oxygen.

rows: Largest yield of ATP, around 36-38 molecules per glucose molecule
A complex multi-stage process, so ATP production is comparatively slow
By-products are carbon dioxide and water - not fatiguing and easily removed
Only functions while sufficient oxygen reaches the muscle, so it cannot meet high-intensity demands
Large stores of muscle glycogen and body fat supply energy for a long time
Fat as a fuel needs roughly 15% more oxygen to break down than glycogen

sections.heading: The ATP-PC (phosphocreatine) system
sections.specBullet: The ATP-PC energy system

paragraphs: The ATP-PC system is anaerobic - it works without oxygen - and provides energy very rapidly for short, maximal bursts such as a 100m sprint or a heavy single lift.

items.meaning: Working without oxygen.
A high-energy compound stored in the sarcoplasm of the muscle.
The enzyme that detects rising ADP levels during exercise and breaks PC down into creatine and an inorganic phosphate, releasing energy.

blocks.meaning: The energy released is then used in a coupled reaction: energy + ADP + Pi → ATP.

rows: ATP resynthesised very rapidly, ideal for explosive efforts
Very limited PC stores, fuelling maximal exercise for only around 8-10 seconds
PC can only be resynthesised once oxygen is available, during lower-intensity exercise or rest
Stores replenish quickly: around 50% within 30 seconds, full restoration in roughly 2-4 minutes

sections.heading: The anaerobic glycolytic system
sections.specBullet: The anaerobic glycolytic energy system

paragraphs: This system covers high-intensity exercise lasting from around 10 seconds up to roughly 2-3 minutes - once ATP-PC stores are exhausted but demand is still too high to be met aerobically.

It breaks muscle glycogen down into glucose, via the enzyme glycogen phosphorylase, then breaks that glucose down anaerobically to pyruvic acid through glycolysis, for a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose molecule.

items.meaning: The enzyme that converts pyruvic acid into lactic acid when oxygen is not available in sufficient amounts.
The by-product formed instead of pyruvic acid continuing into the aerobic pathway.

rows: ATP resynthesised quickly, allowing high-intensity efforts up to roughly 2-3 minutes
Lactic acid build-up denatures enzymes and interferes with further contraction, contributing to fatigue
Does not depend on oxygen availability
Much smaller ATP yield per glycogen molecule than the aerobic system

sections.heading: The energy continuum
sections.specBullet: The energy continuum and thresholds

items.meaning: How the contribution of the three energy systems changes according to the intensity and duration of an activity. All three operate at once, but one dominates.
The point where PC stores are exhausted and the anaerobic glycolytic system becomes dominant, typically around 10 seconds into a maximal effort.
The point where the anaerobic glycolytic system is exhausted, or lactic acid build-up becomes limiting, and the aerobic system takes over - typically around 3 minutes into continuous exercise.

paragraphs: In activities with continuously changing intensity, such as team games, the balance shifts constantly, moving back and forth along the continuum with the demands of each phase of play.

items.wrong: Only one energy system is working at a time.
items.right: All three operate simultaneously. The question is which one dominates at that moment.

sections.heading: Energy system use and muscle fibre type
sections.specBullet: Relationship between energy systems and fibre type

rows: Can sustain it for a long time
Less efficient, cannot be sustained long

sections.heading: Oxygen consumption during exercise
sections.specBullet: Oxygen consumption, oxygen deficit and VO2 max

items.meaning: The amount of oxygen used to produce ATP, usually measured as VO2 - the volume of oxygen consumed per minute.
The shortfall at the start of exercise, where oxygen consumption cannot rise instantly to meet demand because the cardiovascular and respiratory systems take time to respond.
The maximum volume of oxygen the body can take up and use per minute - the ceiling of aerobic capacity.
Where oxygen demand exceeds VO2 max for the whole duration of a maximal effort, used as an indicator of anaerobic capacity.

paragraphs: During the oxygen deficit the muscles rely on anaerobic sources - stored ATP, PC, and anaerobic glycolysis - to make up the shortfall while oxygen delivery catches up. In submaximal aerobic exercise, a steady state of oxygen consumption is then reached.

sections.heading: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC)
sections.specBullet: EPOC and recovery

items.meaning: The extra oxygen used during recovery, while consumption remains elevated above resting levels. Sometimes called oxygen debt.
The rapid initial stage, where oxygen restores ATP and phosphocreatine stores and resaturates myoglobin. Largely complete within 2-4 minutes, with roughly 50% of PC restored in about 30 seconds.
The longer stage, where oxygen helps remove lactic acid, restore glycogen stores, maintain the raised breathing and heart rate delivering that oxygen, and deal with raised body temperature.
The conversion of lactic acid back to glucose and glycogen in the liver.

items: Oxidation into carbon dioxide and water, for use as an energy source
Conversion back to glucose and glycogen in the liver - the Cori cycle
Conversion into protein
Excretion in sweat and urine

sections.heading: Glycogen replenishment
sections.specBullet: Glycogen replenishment after exercise

paragraphs: Glycogen is the main fuel for both the aerobic and anaerobic glycolytic systems, so replenishing it is an important part of recovery. How long it takes depends on the type and intensity of exercise and how much carbohydrate is eaten afterwards - after a marathon it may take several days, while after shorter, higher-intensity work a significant amount returns more quickly.

rows: High-carbohydrate meal, ideally with protein in roughly a 3:1 carbohydrate to protein ratio

sections.heading: Lactate threshold and OBLA
sections.specBullet: Lactate threshold and OBLA

items.meaning: The point at which lactic acid begins to accumulate in the blood faster than it can be removed.
The point at which blood lactate rises sharply above resting levels, typically defined as around 4 millimoles per litre.
A training adaptation that helps neutralise the acidity of lactic acid, allowing higher lactate levels to be sustained.

paragraphs: Lactate threshold is usually expressed as a percentage of VO2 max. Well-trained individuals have a higher threshold - as high as 70-90% of VO2 max in elite endurance performers, against around 50-60% untrained - so they can work at a higher relative intensity before lactic acid accumulates rapidly.

Elite sprint and power athletes tend to have greater anaerobic capacity and tolerance of high lactate than endurance athletes, partly through buffering, letting them work at higher intensities for longer before fatigue.

items: Exercise intensity: higher intensity means greater reliance on fast twitch fibres and anaerobic glycolysis, so lactate accumulates faster
Muscle fibre type recruited: fast twitch fibres produce more lactate than slow twitch
The rate of lactate removal relative to production
Fitness of the performer: trained individuals have more mitochondria, greater capillary density and a better capacity to use lactic acid as fuel, all delaying accumulation

sections.heading: VO2 max and aerobic power
sections.specBullet: VO2 max and factors affecting it

items.term: VO2 max (maximal oxygen uptake, or aerobic power)
items.meaning: The maximum volume of oxygen the body can take up and use per minute, usually expressed relative to body mass in ml/kg/min.

Maximum cardiac output, stroke volume, greater heart range, oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, number and size of mitochondria, capillarisation around the muscles, myoglobin content and lactate tolerance.
Aerobic endurance training - continuous, fartlek, interval - can improve VO2 max over a training period.
Inherited physiology sets a limit on how much VO2 max can ultimately be improved by training.
Males generally have a higher VO2 max than females of similar training status, partly due to body composition and haemoglobin levels.
VO2 max tends to decline as the body's systems become less efficient.
A higher percentage of body fat is associated with a lower VO2 max.
Smoking, a sedentary lifestyle and poor diet can all reduce VO2 max.

sections.heading: Measuring energy expenditure
sections.specBullet: Methods of measuring energy expenditure

items.meaning: Measures energy expenditure by analysing the gases exchanged during exercise - oxygen consumed and carbon dioxide produced - with the performer wearing a mask connected to a gas analyser, typically on a treadmill or cycle ergometer.
A small blood sample, often from the ear lobe or fingertip, analysed with a handheld device to measure blood lactate concentration.
The ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed (VCO2/VO2), calculated from the gases measured during indirect calorimetry.

paragraphs: Indirect calorimetry gives an accurate estimate of energy expenditure and can also identify which fuel, fat or carbohydrate, is predominantly being used. Lactate sampling is used to assess exercise intensity and training zones, monitor fitness, and track improvements in lactate threshold over repeated testing.

rows: Predominantly fat as a fuel source
Predominantly carbohydrate as a fuel source
Anaerobic respiration occurring, with more carbon dioxide produced than oxygen consumed

sections.heading: Specialist training methods
sections.specBullet: Impact of specialist training methods on energy systems

items.meaning: Training above around 2,500m where the partial pressure of oxygen is lower, reducing the diffusion gradient between the alveoli and the blood so less oxygen saturates onto haemoglobin. This stimulates production of more red blood cells.

rows: Increased red blood cell count and haemoglobin level
Hard to train at the same intensity due to reduced oxygen availability
A detraining effect on other fitness components
Enhanced lactate tolerance, improving aerobic performance and VO2 max at sea level
Benefits lost relatively quickly on return to sea level
Possible psychological problems such as homesickness

items.meaning: Periods of high-intensity exercise interspersed with lower-intensity exercise or rest. Variables include the duration and intensity of the work interval, the duration of recovery, and the number of intervals.
Training designed to increase muscular power through explosive activities such as bounding, hopping, depth jumps and medicine ball work, relying on fast twitch fibres and anaerobic energy provision.

Training to improve moving quickly, changing direction efficiently and reacting to a stimulus, combining speed, coordination, balance and flexibility - drills such as zig-zag runs and agility ladders.

paragraphs: HIIT trains both the aerobic and anaerobic glycolytic systems, since short bursts of maximal or near-maximal work are followed by lower-intensity recovery that allows partial replenishment of PC stores and removal of some lactic acid before the next interval. SAQ, because it involves maximal-effort movements, is fuelled predominantly by the anaerobic systems.

items: Eccentric (pre-loading/pre-stretching) phase: the muscle lengthens under tension as it prepares to produce force, such as on landing from a jump
Amortisation phase: the brief transition between eccentric and concentric. It must be as short as possible, or the elastic energy stored in the eccentric phase is lost as heat
Concentric (muscle contraction) phase: the stored elastic energy produces a forceful, explosive contraction - the upward jump or throw

paragraphs: Those three phases are the stretch-shortening cycle, which is what every plyometric exercise is built around.
